data.life_detail_en: In Germany people often put unwanted things outside with a note, "Zu verschenken" ("free to take"): anyone passing can take them. You can't leave the box out long: the town may treat it as trash and fine you.

data.book_note_en: The rule goes into the "Spell Book" once it is "solid" (after reviews).
data.voice_en: Every thing word has a gender: der, die or das. When you name a thing for the first time, you use "a": ein for der- and das-words, eine (with -e) for die-words. English has one "a" for all.

ch03_L8_why_2.prompt_en: Why "Er funktioniert nicht" and not "Sie funktioniert nicht"?
ch03_L8_why_2.answer_en: er replaces a der-word, for example der Computer.
distractors_en: er means "she": that's for the mouse.
er is only for people, not for things.

ch03_L8_why_3.answer_en: A town has one train station, and both know which: der Bahnhof.
distractors_en: der is only for big buildings in town.
ein is only for questions, and this is an answer.

ch03_L8_why_4.prompt_en: Why does the action come first in "Wiederholen Sie bitte"?
ch03_L8_why_4.answer_en: A request with Sie: the action goes first, then Sie.
distractors_en: Sie always goes first in any sentence.
That's only said at the very end of a lesson.

ch03_L8_why_5.answer_en: Katze is a die-word: eine Katze → keine Katze, with -e.
distractors_en: kein is only for people, not for animals.
keine, because the cat is small and there's one.
